Milton Friedman. A twentieth century American economist and public intellectual who championed free-market capitalism and monetarism, challenging Keynesian orthodoxy from the nineteen sixties onward.

Friedman developed monetarism, the theory that inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. It is caused by excess money supply, not by wage-price spirals or demand shocks. Control the money supply, and you control inflation. This placed monetary policy at the center of economic management, challenging the Keynesian emphasis on government spending.

He was a fierce critic of Keynesian economics and deficit spending. Government fiscal stimulus, he argued, is ineffective at creating lasting employment and merely distorts market incentives. The role of government should be minimal.

Friedman challenged the Phillips curve, which suggested there was a stable trade-off between inflation and unemployment. He developed the concept of the natural rate of unemployment, arguing that in the long run, the Phillips curve is vertical. Governments cannot persistently reduce unemployment below this natural rate through inflation. Any attempt to do so just results in higher inflation without lasting employment gains.

In 1962, Friedman wrote Capitalism and Freedom, a manifesto for minimal government. He advocated for school choice, allowing parents to choose schools with vouchers rather than being assigned to public schools. He championed voluntary exchange and limited government across the board.

He proposed the negative income tax as an alternative to the welfare bureaucracy. Give poor people cash, he argued, rather than complicated programs. This idea preceded modern universal basic income proposals by decades. Friedman served as an advisor to the Chilean government under Pinochet from 1973 to 1988, a period of controversial shock therapy economic reform. His monetarism made him the intellectual opponent of John Maynard Keynes, though by the time Friedman rose to prominence, Keynes was already dead. He shared common ground with Friedrich Hayek, another free-market advocate. Yet his vision of capitalism as inherently liberating stood in complete opposition to Karl Marx's view of it as inherently exploitative, and he clashed with John Kenneth Galbraith, who challenged the free-market gospel from the left.
